    Real cartilage is a thin layer ($a\gg h$) bonded to bone, and the interstitial fluid pressurisation is broad, not peaked — both flatten and spread the pressure below the Hertz cap (§6).

Problems

Thirty problems — ten to reason with, ten to derive, ten to compute — each isolating one idea from the module's spine. Work each out before opening the solution; the computational solutions carry Python-verified numbers.

Conceptual problems

Ten problems to reason with — each isolates one idea from the module's spine. Work out the reasoning before opening the solution.

C1 — undrained vs. drained — one tissue, two stiffnesses. Probes: undrained vs. drained response; the gel time (§3).

Press a cartilage sample with your thumb for a second and it feels firm as hard rubber. Rest a heavy book on the same spot and, over an afternoon, it slowly sinks and stays dented until you lift the book. Same tissue, opposite behaviour. Explain, and name the timescale that separates the two regimes.

solution

Undrained (loading time $\ll\tau$): the fluid has no time to leave, and an incompressible mixture with trapped fluid barely changes volume — it resists almost rigidly. The thumb-press ($\sim1\ \mathrm s$) is undrained, so the tissue feels firm.

Drained (loading time $\gg\tau$): held long enough, the fluid slowly exudes; once it is gone, only the soft drained matrix (aggregate modulus $H_A\sim0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$) resists, so the tissue creeps down and stays dented. The afternoon under a book is drained. (It recovers when unloaded because the osmotic swelling pressure of §2 re-imbibes the fluid.)

The separating timescale is the gel time $\tau\sim h^2/(H_Ak)\sim10^3$–$10^4\ \mathrm s$ (minutes to hours). Firm below it, soft above it — one material, two stiffnesses, set by whether you outrun the drainage.

C2 — why cartilage swells at rest. Probes: fixed charge, Donnan osmosis, and the resting swelling pre-stress (§2).

A freshly excised plug of cartilage, floated in saline, visibly swells; cut a slit in it and the slit gapes open. What in the tissue's composition drives this, and why does it matter mechanically before any external load is applied?

solution

Proteoglycans carry a dense fixed negative charge $c_F$. To keep electroneutrality, mobile counter-ions (mainly $\mathrm{Na^+}$) are held inside at higher concentration than the surrounding bath; that excess ion concentration raises the interstitial osmotic pressure — the Donnan swelling pressure $\pi$ (§2). Water follows osmotically and the solid matrix swells until the collagen network's tension balances $\pi$.

So even with no external load the tissue is pre-stressed: collagen in tension, gel in compression at $\pi\approx0.16\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Mechanically this pre-stress stiffens the surface, resists the very first increment of load, and re-imbibes fluid after unloading (the recovery in C1 and C10). Lose the charge — as in degeneration — and the pre-stress, the surface stiffness, and the recovery all fall together (§8).

C3 — who carries the first instant of load. Probes: incompressibility of the saturated mixture; why $\sigma_E=0$ at $t=0$ (§4).

The moment you step — before any fluid has moved — what fraction of the load does the interstitial fluid carry, and why must it be exactly that fraction, independent of how stiff the solid matrix is?

solution

All of it: $F(0)=1$. The tissue is fully saturated and both phases are nearly incompressible, so the only way to change volume is to expel fluid — which takes time. In the first instant no fluid has left, so the volumetric strain is zero, so the solid strain is zero, so the effective stress $\sigma_E=H_A\varepsilon=0$ — the solid carries nothing, regardless of $H_A$.

The applied traction is balanced entirely by a jump in interstitial pressure $p$. This is why cartilage feels rigid on impact even though its drained modulus is soft (C1): stiffness on the timescale of a footstep is set by fluid incompressibility, not by the matrix.

C4 — slippery standing still. Probes: that biphasic lubrication needs no sliding speed, unlike a fluid-film bearing (§7).

A journal bearing is only slippery once it spins fast enough to float on an oil film; at rest it is metal-on-metal and stiff to start. Cartilage is slippery even when you have been standing still. Explain the difference.

solution

In a hydrodynamic bearing the load-bearing film is generated by motion: oil entrained into a converging wedge builds the pressure, so at $v=0$ there is no film and friction is high. Cartilage does not rely on entrainment. Its load-bearing pressure is the interstitial fluid pressurisation, which exists whenever the tissue is freshly loaded ($F\approx1$), speed or no speed.

Friction acts only on the solid-borne fraction: $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-F)$ (§7). With $F\approx1$ at rest, $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx0$. Only if you stand long enough for the fluid to drain ($F\to0$, minutes–hours, C1) does $\mu$ climb toward the intrinsic $\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}$. Cartilage is a pre-charged pressurised bearing, not a speed-dependent one.

C5 — why the dry calculation is too harsh. Probes: why a thin bonded layer and broad fluid pressurisation flatten the peak below the dry-Hertz cap (§6).

A dry-elastic (Hertz) contact calculation for the tibiofemoral (knee) contact of §6 gives a peak pressure $p_0\approx2.5\ \mathrm{MPa}$. The real cartilage peak is lower and broader. Give two independent reasons the dry calculation overestimates the true peak, and say which of them would also apply, more strongly, to the conforming hip.

solution

(1) Geometry — a thin bonded layer. Hertz assumes two elastic half-spaces free to bulge. Cartilage is a thin layer ($a\gg h$) firmly bonded to stiff subchondral bone, which cannot bulge sideways as a half-space would; the confinement spreads the contact wider and lowers the peak.

(2) Biphasic pressurisation. On the loading timescale the load is carried by interstitial pressure, which is a broad, plateau-like field, not a sharp Hertzian dome.

Both effects redistribute the same total load ($\int p\,2\pi r\,\mathrm dr=R$) over a larger area, so the peak drops (here $\approx2.5\to\approx2.0\ \mathrm{MPa}$) while the mean is essentially unchanged. The figure overlays the two profiles carrying the identical load.

Which applies to the hip. Both, and the first far more strongly. The hip is a conforming ball-in-socket, so its surfaces are congruent over a large area before any load is applied; Hertz, which assumes two convex bodies touching at a point, under-predicts that area badly and over-predicts the peak correspondingly. That is why §6 works the knee — a genuine convex-on-flat contact — and carries over only the load magnitude from Module 3's hip.

C6 — one tissue, two moduli. Probes: the composite origin of cartilage's very different tensile and compressive stiffness (§1).

Cartilage is roughly $20\times$ stiffer in tension than in compression. What microstructural feature accounts for each, and why does the asymmetry make sense for a bearing surface?

solution

Tension is resisted by the collagen fibril network — stiff, high-tensile-modulus fibres ($E_{\mathrm{tens}}\approx12\ \mathrm{MPa}$; Appendix, from a reported range of $10$–$15$) that carry pull like the cords in a tyre. Compression is resisted by the proteoglycan gel and its Donnan swelling — a soft, drained aggregate modulus $H_A\sim0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Fibres buckle under compression but pull taut under tension, so the tissue is soft to squeeze but stiff to stretch.

For a bearing this is ideal: the soft compressive response lets the surfaces conform and spread contact (lowering peak pressure, C5), while the stiff tensile skin resists the hoop and tensile stresses that a conforming, pressurised layer generates — holding the tissue together under the very loads its softness invites.

C7 — relaxation versus creep. Probes: that stress-relaxation (fixed strain) and creep (fixed load) are the same biphasic physics under two boundary conditions (§5).

Compress a plug to a fixed depth and hold: the force you must apply slowly falls. Instead hang a fixed weight on it: the plug slowly sinks. Are these two different material behaviours? Explain both with one mechanism.

solution

One mechanism, two controls. In both, the load is first carried by pressurised fluid ($F\approx1$) which then drains over $\tau$.

Fixed strain (relaxation): the initial undrained stress is high because the incompressible mixture resists; as fluid leaves, the pressure decays and the stress relaxes toward the drained value $\sigma_\infty=H_A\varepsilon$.

Fixed load (creep): the initial undrained strain is small (stiff); as fluid leaves, the plug deforms further until the drained matrix alone carries the load at $\varepsilon_\infty=\sigma/H_A$.

Same drainage, same $\tau$. Relaxation is the stress transient at fixed strain; creep is the strain transient at fixed stress. The figure shows the falling-stress and rising-strain curves side by side.

C8 — the vicious cycle. Probes: osteoarthritis as a positive-feedback loss of fluid support, not a single failure (§8).

Osteoarthritis is often called "wear and tear," as if the cartilage simply abrades away. Reframe it as a feedback loop, and identify what makes the loop self-amplifying.

solution

The primary mechanical event is loss of fluid load support. Matrix damage (charge loss, collagen disruption) raises the permeability $k$, which shortens the gel time $\tau=h^2/(H_Ak)$ and lets fluid drain faster; $F$ sags.

Lower $F$ means the solid matrix carries more stress and friction rises, $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-F)$. Higher stress and friction abrade and fibrillate the surface, which damages more matrix and raises $k$ further — closing the loop.

Each pass makes the next worse: a positive feedback, not a one-shot failure. The leverage point is anywhere that breaks the loop (restore charge and $\pi$, lower the load, restore $F$). "Wear" is the loop's output, not its cause.

C9 — thin heals faster. Probes: the drainage-path scaling $\tau\propto h^2$ and its clinical reading (§3).

Two cartilage samples of the same tissue, one $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick and one $2\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick, are loaded identically. Which reaches its drained (soft) state sooner, and by what factor? What does this say about where thick cartilage (e.g. the patella) sits on the load-timescale map?

solution

The thinner one drains faster. Since $\tau=h^2/D$ scales as the square of the drainage path, halving $h$ cuts $\tau$ by $4$ (the $2\ \mathrm{mm}$ plug is $4\times$ slower). Physically, fluid in the thick plug must travel twice as far to reach a drained surface, and diffusion time goes as distance squared.

Clinically, thick cartilage keeps $F$ high over longer loading times — better sustained protection during prolonged stance — but relaxes and recovers more slowly, so it depends more on adequate unloaded recovery periods (C10). Thin, degenerate cartilage (small $h$, large $k$) has a tiny $\tau$ and loses fluid support within a step or two.

C10 — why you are taller in the morning. Probes: reversible daily fluid loss and osmotic recovery; the swelling pressure as the reset (§2, §4).

People are measurably taller in the morning than at night (partly from spinal cartilage and discs). Explain the daily cycle, why it is normally reversible, and what would make it stop reversing.

solution

Under a day of loading, cartilage and discs slowly exude fluid (drained creep, C1/C7) and thin — you lose height. Unloaded overnight, the Donnan swelling pressure $\pi$ (§2) osmotically re-imbibes water and the tissue recovers thickness by morning.

The cycle is reversible precisely because the fixed-charge-driven $\pi$ survives the day; it is the restoring force. It stops reversing if the charge is lost (degeneration): with $\pi$ gone, exuded fluid is not drawn back, the tissue stays thin, $F$ cannot recover between loadings, and repeated cycles ratchet down (K9). Recovery, not just loading, is a physiological requirement.

Derivational problems

Ten derivations — show every step; the boxed line is the result to reach.

D1 — one- versus two-sided drainage. Probes: eigenfunctions and boundary conditions; the drainage path (§3).

The confined-compression gel time for a plug of thickness $h$ drained on one face (impermeable base) is $\tau_1=4h^2/(\pi^2D)$, $D=H_Ak$. Now make both faces permeable. Derive the new fundamental gel time and the factor by which it changes, and explain it physically.

solution

The pressure obeys $\partial p/\partial t=D\,\partial^2p/\partial z^2$; the slowest (fundamental) relaxation mode sets the gel time, $\tau=1/(D\lambda_1^2)$, where $\lambda_1$ is the smallest eigenvalue admitted by the boundary conditions.

One-sided (impermeable base $\partial p/\partial z=0$ at $z=0$, drained $p=0$ at $z=h$): admissible modes are $\cos(\lambda z)$ with $\lambda_n=(2n+1)\pi/2h$; the fundamental is $\lambda_1=\pi/2h$, giving $\tau_1=1/(D\lambda_1^2)=4h^2/(\pi^2D)$.

Two-sided (drained at both $z=0$ and $z=h$): modes are $\sin(n\pi z/h)$ with $\lambda_n=n\pi/h$; the fundamental is $\lambda_1=\pi/h$, giving $\tau_2=1/(D\lambda_1^2)=h^2/(\pi^2D)$.

$$\frac{\tau_2}{\tau_1}=\frac{(\pi/2h)^2}{(\pi/h)^2}=\frac14.$$

Draining both faces makes the tissue relax four times faster. Physically, fluid now escapes from both surfaces, so the farthest any fluid must travel to a drain is halved ($h\to h/2$); since $\tau\propto(\text{drainage path})^2$, the time drops by $4$.

D2 — derive the swelling pressure. Probes: Donnan equilibrium plus electroneutrality → the ideal osmotic swelling pressure (§2).

A charged tissue with fixed-charge density $c_F$ (per unit fluid volume) sits in a bath of monovalent salt at concentration $c_0$. Assuming ideal (dilute) solutions, derive the interstitial swelling pressure $\pi$, and evaluate it for $c_F=0.2\ \mathrm M$, $c_0=0.15\ \mathrm M$, $\Theta=310\ \mathrm K$.

solution

Let the interstitial mobile cation and anion concentrations be $c_+,c_-$. Two conditions apply.

Electroneutrality inside (the fixed charge is negative): $c_+=c_-+c_F$.

Donnan equilibrium (salt chemical potential equal inside and out): $c_+c_-=c_0^2$.

Eliminate: $c_-(c_-+c_F)=c_0^2\Rightarrow c_-=\tfrac12(\sqrt{c_F^2+4c_0^2}-c_F)$ and $c_+=\tfrac12(\sqrt{c_F^2+4c_0^2}+c_F)$.

The osmotic (swelling) pressure is the van 't Hoff pressure of the excess total mobile-ion concentration inside relative to the bath:

$$\boxed{\;\pi=R_g\Theta\big[(c_++c_-)-2c_0\big]=R_g\Theta\big[\sqrt{c_F^2+4c_0^2}-2c_0\big].\;}$$

Numbers: $\sqrt{0.2^2+4(0.15)^2}=\sqrt{0.13}=0.3606\ \mathrm M$; minus $0.30\ \mathrm M=0.0606\ \mathrm M=60.6\ \mathrm{mol/m^3}$. With $R_g\Theta=8.314\times310=2577\ \mathrm{J/mol}$: $\pi=2577\times60.6\approx1.56\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\approx0.16\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

Check the limits: $\pi\to0$ as $c_F\to0$ (an uncharged gel does not swell), and for $c_F\ll c_0$ expanding the root gives $\pi=2R_g\Theta c_0\big[\sqrt{1+c_F^2/(4c_0^2)}-1\big]\approx R_g\Theta\,c_F^2/(4c_0)$ — quadratic in the fixed charge, matching §2. (At $c_F=0.01\ \mathrm M$, $c_0=0.15\ \mathrm M$ the exact formula gives $429.4\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and this limit $429.6\ \mathrm{Pa}$; a $2c_0$ denominator would give $859\ \mathrm{Pa}$, twice too much.) The healthy operating point $c_F=0.2\ \mathrm M$ is not in that regime — it sits above $c_0$ — which is why K10 finds a local log-slope of $1.83$ there rather than the asymptotic $2$.

D3 — derive the consolidation equation. Probes: mass balance + Darcy + linear elasticity → the governing diffusion PDE (§3).

For 1-D confined compression along $z$, with solid displacement $u(z,t)$, derive the governing equation $\partial u/\partial t=H_Ak\,\partial^2u/\partial z^2$. State each assumption.

solution

Take a slab $[z,z+\mathrm dz]$ and assume: incompressible solid and fluid, full saturation, small strain, constant $k$ and $H_A$, 1-D confined geometry, and linear (Darcy) flow.

(i) Kinematics. Strain $\varepsilon=\partial u/\partial z$.

(ii) Effective stress at constant load. Total stress $\sigma=\sigma_E-p$ with $\sigma_E=H_A\varepsilon$. Under a suddenly-applied constant total stress, $\partial\sigma/\partial t=0$, so $$H_A\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}.\quad(\mathrm A)$$

(iii) Continuity + Darcy. With incompressible constituents, the rate of volumetric strain equals the divergence of the relative fluid flux $q$; Darcy gives $q=-k\,\partial p/\partial z$, so $$\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial q}{\partial z}=k\,\frac{\partial^2p}{\partial z^2}.\quad(\mathrm B)$$

Combine. Substituting (A) into (B), $\partial p/\partial t=H_Ak\,\partial^2p/\partial z^2$. Because $p$ and $u$ are linearly related through (A) and $\varepsilon=\partial u/\partial z$, the displacement obeys the same equation:

$$\boxed{\;\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=H_Ak\,\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial z^2},\qquad D\equiv H_Ak.\;}$$

It is a diffusion equation; the diffusivity $D=H_Ak$ carries the whole consolidation timescale.

D4 — short-time fluid support. Probes: the early-time square-root law from the diffusion similarity solution (§4).

For $T=Dt/h^2\ll1$, show that the fluid load support behaves as $F\approx1-2\sqrt{T/\pi}$, and explain why the correction is $\sqrt T$ rather than linear in $T$.

solution

At short time only a thin drained boundary layer near the permeable surface has formed; the rest of the plug is still fully pressurised. The diffusion penetration depth grows as $\delta\sim\sqrt{Dt}$ (the similarity solution of the half-space diffusion problem).

The lost support is proportional to the drained fraction $\delta/h\sim\sqrt{Dt}/h=\sqrt T$. Evaluating the half-space surface deficit gives the constant $2/\sqrt\pi$, so $$F\approx1-2\sqrt{T/\pi}.$$

The $\sqrt T$ (not $T$) is the fingerprint of diffusion: distance grows as the square root of time, so the drained layer — and the support deficit — grows as $\sqrt t$. The figure shows this line hugging the exact series near the origin and parting later.

D5 — the eigenvalue series. Probes: separation of variables giving the mode set and the slowest-mode gel time (§4).

Proposition 3.1 quotes the mode set for one-sided drainage. Re-derive it from scratch: find the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of the pressure diffusion problem, show that the depth-average of the series is $F(T)=\sum_n 2/\lambda_n^2\,e^{-\lambda_n^2T}$, and identify which single mode sets the gel time and why the others are invisible after a fraction of one $\tau$.

solution

Separate $p=Z(z)\,e^{-D\mu^2t}$: then $Z''+\mu^2Z=0$. The boundary conditions select the modes:

$Z'(0)=0$ (no flux at the sealed base) $\Rightarrow Z=\cos(\mu z)$; $Z(h)=0$ (drained) $\Rightarrow \cos(\mu h)=0\Rightarrow \mu_nh=(2n+1)\tfrac\pi2$, i.e. $\lambda_n\equiv\mu_nh=(2n+1)\pi/2$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$

Expanding the uniform initial pressure in these modes and integrating over depth to get the load support gives the coefficients $2/\lambda_n^2$, so $$F(T)=\sum_n\frac{2}{\lambda_n^2}\,e^{-\lambda_n^2T},\qquad T=\frac{Dt}{h^2}.$$

Late in time the slowest mode dominates: $n=0$, $\lambda_0=\pi/2$, giving $\tau=1/(D\mu_0^2)=4h^2/(\pi^2D)$ — the gel time of D1. The figure plots the first three cosine modes; the flat $n=0$ mode (peak at the sealed base) is the long-lived one.

Why the others are invisible. Mode $n$ decays as $e^{-\lambda_n^{2}T}$ with $\lambda_n^{2}=(2n+1)^{2}\pi^{2}/4$, so at $T=1$ the $n=1$ mode is down by $e^{-(9-1)\pi^{2}/4}=e^{-19.7}\approx3\times10^{-9}$ relative to $n=0$. After a fraction of a gel time the series is a single exponential; that is why $\tau=4h^{2}/(\pi^{2}D)$ is a sharp number and not a fitted one.

D6 — why $\tau$ scales as $h^2$. Probes: nondimensionalising the PDE shows $\tau$ is a fixed value of $T=Dt/h^2$ (§5).

Without solving the series, show from the governing equation alone that the gel time must scale as $h^2/D$, and that changing $h$ only rescales the time axis.

solution

Nondimensionalise. Let $\zeta=z/h$ and $T=Dt/h^2$. Then $\partial u/\partial t=D\,\partial^2u/\partial z^2$ becomes $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial T}=\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\zeta^2},$$ with no parameters left — $h$ and $D$ have vanished. So the entire relaxation history is a universal function of $T$ only, $F=\Phi(T)$.

The gel time is defined by some fixed fraction of relaxation (say $F=\tfrac12$), reached at a fixed $T=T_0$ (a pure number). Undoing the scaling, $t_{1/2}=T_0\,h^2/D$, i.e. $\tau\propto h^2/D$.

Doubling $h$ stretches the physical time axis by $4$ with the curve otherwise unchanged: every thickness collapses onto one master curve in $T$ (the figure) — the $\tau\propto h^2$ result, obtained without any series.

D7 — the Hertz exponents. Probes: the sphere-on-plane scaling of contact radius and peak pressure with load and radius (§6).

For a rigid sphere of effective radius $R_{\rm eff}$ pressed with force $N$ into an elastic half-space of reduced modulus $E^*$, derive the scalings $a\propto(NR_{\rm eff}/E^*)^{1/3}$ and $p_0\propto N/a^2$, and hence how $a$ and $p_0$ change if $R_{\rm eff}$ doubles at fixed $N$.

solution

Geometry. For a sphere the interpenetration depth and contact radius satisfy $\delta\approx a^2/R$.

Elastic contact. Force relates to modulus, radius and depth by $N\sim E^*a\,\delta\sim E^*a\,(a^2/R)=E^*a^3/R$. Solving, $$a\sim\Big(\frac{NR}{E^*}\Big)^{1/3}\propto N^{1/3}R^{1/3}.$$

Peak pressure. $p_0=\dfrac{3N}{2\pi a^2}\propto\dfrac{N}{a^2}\propto N\,(NR/E^*)^{-2/3}=N^{1/3}(E^*)^{2/3}R^{-2/3}.$

At fixed load $N$: $a\propto R^{1/3}$ (doubling $R$ raises $a$ by $2^{1/3}\approx1.26$) and $p_0\propto R^{-2/3}$ (falls by $2^{-2/3}\approx0.63$). A more conforming (larger-$R$) joint spreads the contact and lowers the peak — the geometric half of why congruent joints protect cartilage. The figure plots both scalings.

D8 — the friction law. Probes: deriving $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-F)$ from the load partition (§7).

The normal load $N$ across a cartilage contact is shared between interstitial fluid pressure and solid–solid contact. Taking friction to act only on the solid-borne load with intrinsic coefficient $\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}$, derive the effective friction coefficient in terms of the fluid load fraction $F$.

solution

Partition the normal load: fluid carries $N_f=FN$, solid contact carries $N_s=(1-F)N$.

Interstitial fluid pressure is essentially inviscid on this scale and transmits negligible shear, so the only frictional resistance comes from the solid contact: the tangential force is $f=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}N_s=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-F)N$.

The measured (effective) coefficient is $$\boxed{\;\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac fN=\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-F).\;}$$

Limits: fresh load $F\to1\Rightarrow\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\to0$ (the vanishing-friction pressurised regime); fully drained $F\to0\Rightarrow\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\to\mu_{\mathrm{eq}}$ (the intrinsic solid-on-solid value, $\sim0.15$). Cartilage lives near the top limit because $F$ stays high for the duration of normal loading (D4), which is why measured $\mu\sim0.005$–$0.02$.

D9 — the equilibrium creep strain. Probes: that the long-time drained strain is set by the aggregate modulus alone (§5).

A confined plug under a constant applied stress $\sigma$ creeps. Show that the final (drained) strain is $\varepsilon_\infty=\sigma/H_A$, independent of permeability, and say what $k$ does control.

solution

At equilibrium nothing flows, so $q=0$, and Darcy $q=-k\,\partial p/\partial z=0$ with drained boundaries forces $p=0$ throughout: the fluid carries none of the load.

The entire applied stress is then borne by the solid effective stress: $\sigma=\sigma_E=H_A\varepsilon_\infty$, hence $$\boxed{\;\varepsilon_\infty=\sigma/H_A.\;}$$

Permeability $k$ has dropped out — it cannot affect the endpoint, only the path to it: $k$ (through $D=H_Ak$ and $\tau=h^2/D$) sets how fast the strain climbs to $\varepsilon_\infty$, not its value. Two tissues with the same $H_A$ but different $k$ creep to the same final dent, one faster than the other. The figure shows $\varepsilon(t)/\varepsilon_\infty\to1$.

D10 — when does degeneration run away. Probes: a loop-gain (linear-stability) condition for the OA feedback (§8).

Model the degeneration cascade of C8 as a feedback loop: a small drop $\delta F$ in fluid support produces extra damage that further lowers $F$. Writing the per-cycle amplification as a loop gain $G$, state the condition for a small perturbation to heal versus run away, and interpret $G$.

solution

Let the perturbation to the fluid-support deficit after $n$ cycles be $x_n$. Each pass round the loop multiplies it: $$x_{n+1}=G\,x_n\quad\Rightarrow\quad x_n=G^n\,x_0.$$

If $G\lt1$ the deficit decays geometrically — the tissue heals and returns to homeostasis. If $G\gt1$ it grows without bound — runaway degeneration. The threshold is $G=1$.

The loop gain is the product of the sensitivities around the cycle, written in logarithmic variables so that each factor is a dimensionless elasticity: $$G=\frac{\partial\ln d}{\partial\ln k}\cdot\frac{\partial\ln(\text{wear rate})}{\partial\ln d}\cdot\frac{\partial\ln k}{\partial\ln(\text{wear})},\qquad d\equiv1-F.$$Only the first factor belongs to this module, and it is exact: D4 gives $d=2\sqrt{H_Akt/(\pi h^2)}\propto\sqrt k$, so $\partial\ln d/\partial\ln k=\tfrac12$ (§8 checks it against the full series). The other two are mechanobiological and are assumed, not derived, here; $G\gt1$ therefore requires them to supply a combined gain above $2$.

Interventions — lower load, restore charge and $F$, reduce friction — all act by pushing $G$ below $1$. The inset contrasts a decaying ($G\lt1$) and a growing ($G\gt1$) response.

Computational problems

Ten to compute — every number is reproduced by the copy-buttoned Python beneath its solution.

K1 — diffusivity, gel time, and fluid support. Probes: $D=H_Ak$; $F(T)=\sum 2/\lambda_n^2e^{-\lambda_n^2T}$ with $T=Dt/h^2$; the footstep-vs-$\tau$ separation (§3, §4).

A cartilage plug has thickness $h=1.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, aggregate modulus $H_A=0.8\ \mathrm{MPa}$, and permeability $k=2\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^4/(N\,s)}$. (a) Compute the consolidation diffusivity $D$ and the gel time $\tau=h^2/D$. (b) During a $t_{\rm load}=0.5\ \mathrm s$ footstep, estimate the fluid load support $F$. (c) Degeneration triples the permeability; recompute $\tau$ and $F(\text{footstep})$ and comment.

solution

(a) $D=H_Ak=(0.8\times10^6)(2\times10^{-15})=1.6\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$; $\tau=h^2/D=(1.5\times10^{-3})^2/1.6\times10^{-9}=1.41\times10^{3}\ \mathrm s\approx23\ \mathrm{min}$.

(b) $T=t_{\rm load}/\tau=3.6\times10^{-4}\ll1$; the series gives $F=0.979$ (short-time $F\approx1-2\sqrt{T/\pi}=0.979$). The fluid carries $\approx98\%$.

(c) $k\to6\times10^{-15}$: $D=4.8\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, $\tau=469\ \mathrm s\approx7.8\ \mathrm{min}$; $F(\text{footstep})=0.963$.

Comment. Tripling permeability barely dents single-step support ($0.98\to0.96$): a footstep is far shorter than even the degraded gel time. The danger is not that one step fails — it is cumulative. With $\tau$ cut, fluid drains between steps faster than §2's osmotic swelling can re-imbibe it, so $F$ sags over sustained and repeated loading (§8), and the rising friction ($\mu_{\rm eff}=\mu_{\rm eq}(1-F)$ climbs from $0.003$ toward $0.006$ here, and further as $F$ sags) abrades the surface. The reassuring single-step number hides a cyclic failure.

import numpy as np
h, HA = 1.5e-3, 0.8e6


def F(k, t=0.5, N=2000):
    D = HA*k
    T = D*t/h**2
    lam = (2*np.arange(N)+1)*np.pi/2
    return D, h**2/D, np.sum(2/lam**2 * np.exp(-lam**2*T))


for k in (2e-15, 6e-15):
    D, tau, Fv = F(k)
    print(f"k={k:.0e}  tau={tau:6.0f} s  F(0.5 s)={Fv:.3f}")
# k=2e-15  tau=  1406 s  F(0.5 s)=0.979
# k=6e-15  tau=   469 s  F(0.5 s)=0.963
K2 — the swelling pressure and its collapse. Probes: the Donnan formula; the fast (super-linear) sensitivity to charge loss (§2).

Using $\pi=R_g\Theta[\sqrt{c_F^2+4c_0^2}-2c_0]$ with $c_0=0.15\ \mathrm M$, $\Theta=310\ \mathrm K$: (a) compute $\pi$ for healthy $c_F=0.2\ \mathrm M$. (b) Degeneration halves the fixed charge to $c_F=0.1\ \mathrm M$; recompute and give the fractional loss of swelling pressure. (c) Comment on the mechanical consequence.

solution

(a) $\sqrt{0.2^2+4(0.15)^2}=\sqrt{0.13}=0.3606\ \mathrm M$; minus $0.30=0.0606\ \mathrm M=60.6\ \mathrm{mol/m^3}$; $\pi=2577\times60.6=1.56\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}=0.156\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

(b) $\sqrt{0.1^2+4(0.15)^2}=\sqrt{0.10}=0.3162\ \mathrm M$; minus $0.30=0.0162\ \mathrm M=16.2\ \mathrm{mol/m^3}$; $\pi=2577\times16.2=4.18\times10^4=0.042\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Loss $=(0.156-0.042)/0.156=73\%$.

(c) Halving the charge cuts the swelling pre-stress by nearly three-quarters. The tissue loses the pre-stress that stiffens its surface and re-imbibes fluid, so both its instantaneous stiffness and its overnight recovery (C10) collapse — the entry point of the C8 cascade.

import numpy as np
RgTheta, c0 = 8.314*310, 0.15
def pi(cF): return RgTheta*(np.sqrt(cF**2 + 4*c0**2) - 2*c0)*1e3  # Pa


for cF in (0.2, 0.1):
    print(f"c_F={cF} M  pi={pi(cF)/1e6:.3f} MPa")
print(f"loss = {100*(pi(0.2)-pi(0.1))/pi(0.2):.0f}%")
# c_F=0.2 M  pi=0.156 MPa
# c_F=0.1 M  pi=0.042 MPa
# loss = 73%
K3 — the knee contact patch. Probes: computing contact radius, peak and mean pressure, and testing them against Module 3 (§6).

Carry the lower-limb joint reaction $R=1715\ \mathrm N$ (Module 3) onto the tibiofemoral contact of §6: a condyle of effective radius $R_{\rm eff}=30\ \mathrm{mm}$ on cartilage of reduced modulus $E^*=6.67\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Compute (a) the contact radius $a=(3RR_{\rm eff}/4E^*)^{1/3}$, (b) the peak Hertz pressure $p_0=3R/(2\pi a^2)$, (c) the mean pressure $\bar p=R/(\pi a^2)$, and compare $\bar p$ with the Module 3 estimate of $1.7\ \mathrm{MPa}$. (d) $R_{\rm eff}$ was chosen as a representative condylar curvature, not measured. Using D7's exponents, say how far $R_{\rm eff}$ would have to be wrong to move $\bar p$ by $20\%$, and hence how much the agreement in (c) is worth.

solution

(a) $a=\big(3\cdot1715\cdot0.03/(4\cdot6.67\times10^6)\big)^{1/3}=(5.785\times10^{-6})^{1/3}=1.795\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m=18.0\ \mathrm{mm}$.

(b) $p_0=3\cdot1715/(2\pi(1.795\times10^{-2})^2)=5145/(2.024\times10^{-3})=2.54\times10^6=2.54\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

(c) $\bar p=1715/(\pi(1.795\times10^{-2})^2)=1715/(1.012\times10^{-3})=1.69\times10^6=1.69\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

The Hertz mean ($1.69\ \mathrm{MPa}$) agrees with the Module 3 force-over-area estimate ($1.7\ \mathrm{MPa}$) to two figures. The peak is $\tfrac32\times$ the mean; the biphasic flattening of C5 brings the true peak down toward $\approx2.0\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

(d) From D7, $a\propto R_{\rm eff}^{1/3}$ at fixed load, so $\bar p=R/(\pi a^2)\propto R_{\rm eff}^{-2/3}$. A $20\%$ change in $\bar p$ therefore needs $R_{\rm eff}$ to change by $1.2^{-3/2}=0.76$ or $0.8^{-3/2}=1.40$ — that is, a condylar radius of $23$ or $42\ \mathrm{mm}$ instead of $30$, both inside the real anatomical spread. So (c) is a consistency check, not an independent confirmation: it says the two models are compatible given a plausible curvature, not that the curvature is right. The genuinely independent content of the Hertz calculation is the shape — the $\tfrac32$ peak-to-mean ratio, which follows from the cap alone and is untouched by $R_{\rm eff}$.

import numpy as np
R, Reff, Estar = 1715.0, 0.03, 6.67e6
a = (3*R*Reff/(4*Estar))**(1/3)
p0 = 3*R/(2*np.pi*a**2)
pbar = R/(np.pi*a**2)
print(f"a={a*1e3:.1f} mm  p0={p0/1e6:.2f} MPa  pbar={pbar/1e6:.2f} MPa")
# a=18.0 mm  p0=2.54 MPa  pbar=1.69 MPa
K4 — stress relaxation by finite differences. Probes: an explicit FD solution of the consolidation PDE; the undrained peak and the $h^2$ time (§5).

Solve the 1-D consolidation equation numerically (explicit finite differences) for a plug ramped to strain $\varepsilon_0$ and held. Confirm the stress decays from an undrained peak to $\sigma_\infty=H_A\varepsilon_0$ over a few $\tau$, and that the relaxation time scales as $h^2$.

solution

Discretise $\partial p/\partial t=D\,\partial^2p/\partial z^2$ on $N$ depth nodes with $p=0$ at the drained face and $\partial p/\partial z=0$ (a mirror node) at the sealed base. The total stress is $\sigma(t)=H_A\varepsilon_0\big(1+\langle p\rangle\big)$ with the pressure normalised to its undrained value, so $\sigma$ starts at $2H_A\varepsilon_0$ and falls to $H_A\varepsilon_0$. The explicit step is stable for $r=D\,\mathrm dt/\mathrm dz^2\le\tfrac12$. Running it: $\sigma$ starts at $0.119\ \mathrm{MPa}$ and ends at $0.0600\ \mathrm{MPa}=H_A\varepsilon_0$ exactly. Because the three thicknesses share one time step in seconds, they are three genuinely different computations (Courant number $r=0.4,\ 0.1,\ 0.025$), and yet the half-relaxation time divided by $h^2$ comes out at $3.3352\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{s/m^2}$ for $h=1,2$ and $4\ \mathrm{mm}$ alike — the $h^2$ law to five figures, computed rather than asserted.

The stress starts elevated (undrained, the pressure supports extra load), then $\langle p\rangle\to0$ and $\sigma\to H_A\varepsilon_0$. Because the equation is parameter-free in $T=Dt/h^2$ (D6), doubling $h$ quadruples the real relaxation time while leaving the shape fixed. The figure shows the peak-then-decay.

import numpy as np

h0, HA, k, eps0 = 2e-3, 0.6e6, 1e-15, 0.10
D = HA*k
# ONE fixed time step in seconds, used at every h, so that the three runs
# below are genuinely different computations and not one rescaled.
DT = 0.4*(1e-3/60)**2/D


def relax(h, N=60, ncycle=3.0):
    """Confined relaxation at held strain eps0: (t, sigma, tau)."""
    tau = h**2/D
    dz = h/N
    r = D*DT/dz**2          # 0.4, 0.1, 0.025 for h = 1, 2, 4 mm; all <= 1/2
    p = np.ones(N + 1)      # uniform initial pressure (undrained)
    p[-1] = 0.0             # drained top face
    t, sig = [], []
    for n in range(int(ncycle*tau/DT) + 1):
        t.append(n*DT)
        # total stress = drained elastic stress + mean pore pressure,
        # both referred to the held strain eps0
        sig.append(HA*eps0*(1.0 + p.mean()))
        lap = p[2:] - 2*p[1:-1] + p[:-2]
        p[1:-1] += r*lap
        p[0] = p[1]         # sealed base: zero flux (mirror node)
        p[-1] = 0.0
    return np.array(t), np.array(sig), tau


# (i) the stress decays from an undrained peak to HA*eps0
t, sig, tau = relax(h0)
print(f"tau={tau:.0f} s  sigma_peak={sig[0]/1e6:.3f} MPa  "
      f"sigma_end={sig[-1]/1e6:.4f} MPa  HA*eps0={HA*eps0/1e6:.4f} MPa")

# (ii) the relaxation time scales as h^2
print("h (mm)   t_half (s)   t_half / h^2")
for h in (1e-3, 2e-3, 4e-3):
    t, sig, tau = relax(h)
    half = sig[-1] + 0.5*(sig[0] - sig[-1])
    th = t[np.argmax(sig <= half)]
    print(f"  {h*1e3:.0f}      {th:8.1f}      {th/h**2:.4e}")
# tau=6667 s  sigma_peak=0.119 MPa  sigma_end=0.0600 MPa  HA*eps0=0.0600 MPa
# h (mm)   t_half (s)   t_half / h^2
#   1         333.5      3.3352e+08
#   2        1334.1      3.3352e+08
#   4        5336.3      3.3352e+08
K5 — footstep versus a long stand. Probes: evaluating $F$ for two very different loading durations (§4).

For healthy cartilage ($h=2\ \mathrm{mm}$, $H_A=0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$, $k=10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^4/(N\,s)}$), compute the fluid load support $F$ for (a) a $0.5\ \mathrm s$ footstep and (b) a $1\ \mathrm h$ stand, using $F(T)=\sum 2/\lambda_n^2e^{-\lambda_n^2T}$, $\lambda_n=(2n+1)\pi/2$, $T=Dt/h^2$.

solution

$D=H_Ak=0.6\times10^6\cdot10^{-15}=6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$; $\tau=h^2/D=(2\times10^{-3})^2/6\times10^{-10}=6.7\times10^3\ \mathrm s$ ($1.9\ \mathrm h$).

(a) $T=0.5/6667=7.5\times10^{-5}$, $F=0.990$: a footstep is carried $\approx99\%$ by fluid.

(b) $T=3600/6667=0.54$, $F=0.214$: after an hour near $\tau$, only $\approx21\%$ is fluid-borne; the solid carries most of the load.

The same tissue is a near-perfect fluid bearing for a step and a nearly drained solid for a long stand — the entire point of the gel time. The figure marks both points on the $F(t)$ curve.

import numpy as np
h, HA, k = 2e-3, 0.6e6, 1e-15
D = HA*k
lam = (2*np.arange(2000)+1)*np.pi/2
def F(t): return np.sum(2/lam**2 * np.exp(-lam**2 * D*t/h**2))


print(f"tau={h**2/D:.0f} s  F(0.5 s)={F(0.5):.3f}  F(1 h)={F(3600):.3f}")
# tau=6667 s  F(0.5 s)=0.990  F(1 h)=0.214
K6 — friction follows the fluid. Probes: mapping the decay of $F$ onto a rising friction coefficient (§7).

With $\mu_{\rm eq}=0.15$ and $\mu_{\rm eff}=\mu_{\rm eq}(1-F)$: (a) compute $\mu_{\rm eff}$ for the footstep ($F=0.990$) and for the $1\ \mathrm h$ stand ($F=0.214$) of K5. (b) Comment on why standing still eventually feels no different, frictionally, from a dry contact.

solution

(a) Footstep: $\mu_{\rm eff}=0.15(1-0.990)=0.0015$. Stand: $\mu_{\rm eff}=0.15(1-0.214)=0.118$.

(b) As you stand and the fluid drains, $F\to0$ and $\mu_{\rm eff}\to\mu_{\rm eq}=0.15$ — the intrinsic solid-on-solid value; the pressurised film that made cartilage $\sim100\times$ slipperier has bled away. Motion re-pressurises the tissue (fluid is re-imbibed under the migrating contact), which is why walking keeps joints slippery but prolonged static loading does not. The figure contrasts cartilage's speed-independent low friction with a fluid-film bearing that needs speed.

mu_eq = 0.15
for label, Fv in (("footstep", 0.990), ("1 h stand", 0.214)):
    print(f"{label:10s} F={Fv:.3f}  mu_eff={mu_eq*(1-Fv):.4f}")
# footstep   F=0.990  mu_eff=0.0015
# 1 h stand  F=0.214  mu_eff=0.1179
K7 — creep to the drained limit. Probes: the equilibrium creep strain and the time to reach it (§5).

For the healthy plug ($h=2\ \mathrm{mm}$, $H_A=0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$, $k=10^{-15}$) under constant stress $\sigma=0.3\ \mathrm{MPa}$: (a) compute the equilibrium creep strain $\varepsilon_\infty=\sigma/H_A$. (b) Using the consolidation series, find the time to reach $90\%$ of $\varepsilon_\infty$.

solution

(a) $\varepsilon_\infty=\sigma/H_A=0.3\times10^6/0.6\times10^6=0.50$ (a large, illustrative strain).

(b) The creep follows $\varepsilon(t)/\varepsilon_\infty=1-\sum_n\frac{8}{(2n+1)^2\pi^2}e^{-\lambda_n^2T}$, $\lambda_n=(2n+1)\pi/2$, $T=Dt/h^2$. Solving $\varepsilon/\varepsilon_\infty=0.9$ gives $T\approx0.85$; with $D=6\times10^{-10}$ and $\tau=h^2/D=6667\ \mathrm s$, $t=T\,h^2/D\approx5.7\times10^3\ \mathrm s\approx1.6\ \mathrm h$.

So the plug reaches most of its creep within a couple of gel times — hours, consistent with the "afternoon under a book" of C1. The figure shows the rising strain approaching the $\sigma/H_A$ plateau.

import numpy as np
h, HA, k, sig = 2e-3, 0.6e6, 1e-15, 0.3e6
D = HA*k
eps_inf = sig/HA
n = np.arange(2000)
lam = (2*n+1)*np.pi/2
def frac(T): return 1 - np.sum(8/((2*n+1)**2*np.pi**2)*np.exp(-lam**2*T))


Ts = np.linspace(1e-3, 2, 20000)
curve = np.array([frac(T) for T in Ts])
T90 = Ts[np.argmin(np.abs(curve - 0.9))]
t90 = T90*h**2/D
print(f"eps_inf={eps_inf:.2f}  T90={T90:.3f}"
      f"  t90={t90:.0f} s = {t90/3600:.2f} h")
# eps_inf=0.50  T90=0.848  t90=5654 s = 1.57 h
K8 — the thickness sweep. Probes: the $\tau\propto h^2$ law across the physiological thickness range (§3).

For $D=6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, tabulate the gel time $\tau=h^2/D$ for $h=0.5,1,2,4\ \mathrm{mm}$ and confirm the slope-2 law (each doubling multiplies $\tau$ by $4$).

solution

$\tau=h^2/D$:

$h=0.5\ \mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow\tau=4.2\times10^2\ \mathrm s$ ($7\ \mathrm{min}$); $h=1\ \mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow1.7\times10^3\ \mathrm s$ ($28\ \mathrm{min}$); $h=2\ \mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow6.7\times10^3\ \mathrm s$ ($1.9\ \mathrm h$); $h=4\ \mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow2.7\times10^4\ \mathrm s$ ($7.4\ \mathrm h$).

Each doubling of $h$ multiplies $\tau$ by $4$ — slope $2$ on log-log. Thin degenerate cartilage relaxes in minutes while thick cartilage protects for hours; the drainage-path-squared law spans nearly two decades over the physiological thickness range. The figure is the straight-line log-log plot.

D = 6e-10
for h in (0.5e-3, 1e-3, 2e-3, 4e-3):
    tau = h**2/D
    print(f"h={h*1e3:.1f} mm  tau={tau:7.0f} s = {tau/60:5.1f} min")
# h=0.5 mm  tau=    417 s =   6.9 min
# h=1.0 mm  tau=   1667 s =  27.8 min
# h=2.0 mm  tau=   6667 s = 111.1 min
# h=4.0 mm  tau=  26667 s = 444.4 min
K9 — how far does incomplete recovery push the joint? Probes: solving a linear recurrence for its fixed point, and finding what incomplete recovery can and cannot cause (§8).

Model repeated load/unload cycles by their fluid-support deficit. One loading of duration $t_{\rm load}$ opens a deficit $\Delta F=1-F(t_{\rm load})$; the following unloaded interval re-imbibes a fraction $r$ of the accumulated deficit, so $d_{n+1}=(1-r)\,(d_n+\Delta F)$ with $d_0=0$. (a) Solve the recurrence for the steady-state peak support $F_\infty$ in closed form. (b) Evaluate it for healthy tissue ($k=10^{-15}$, full recovery $r=1$) and for degraded tissue ($k=10^{-13}$, $r=0.8$), taking $t_{\rm load}=1\ \mathrm s$, $h=2\ \mathrm{mm}$, $H_A=0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$, and contrast them at cycles $1$, $5$ and $20$. (c) Sweep $r$ and find the recovery fraction at which the steady-state friction $\mu_{\rm eff}=\mu_{\rm eq}(1-F_\infty)$ is twice its single-step value. (d) Say what this model does not predict, and what would have to change for it to.

solution

(a) The recurrence $d_{n+1}=(1-r)(d_n+\Delta F)$ is affine with ratio $(1-r)$, so for $r\gt0$ it converges to the fixed point $d_*=(1-r)\Delta F/r$. The deficit at peak load in the steady state is $d_*+\Delta F=\Delta F\big[(1-r)/r+1\big]=\Delta F/r$, so

$$\boxed{\;F_\infty=1-\frac{\Delta F}{r}\;}$$

Incomplete recovery multiplies the single-step deficit by exactly $1/r$ — and by nothing more. The approach is geometric with ratio $(1-r)$, so for $r=0.8$ the plateau is reached to within $1\%$ by cycle 3.

(b) With $D=H_Ak$ and $T=Dt_{\rm load}/h^2$, the series gives $\Delta F=1-F(1\ \mathrm s)=0.0138$ for healthy tissue and $0.1382$ for the hundred-fold-more-permeable degraded tissue (the short-time law of D4 reproduces both exactly: $\Delta F=2\sqrt{T/\pi}$). Healthy tissue has $r=1$, so $d_*=0$ and $F_n=0.9862$ at every cycle — flat. Degraded tissue with $r=0.8$ starts at $F_1=0.8618$ and settles at $F_\infty=1-0.1382/0.8=0.8273$, reached by cycle 5 and unchanged at cycle 20.

(c) Since the steady-state deficit is $\Delta F/r$ and the single-step deficit is $\Delta F$, the friction ratio is exactly $1/r$. It reaches $2$ at $r=0.500$ and $5$ at $r=0.2$: $F_\infty=0.7236$ ($\mu_{\rm eff}=0.0415$) and $F_\infty=0.3090$ ($\mu_{\rm eff}=0.1036$) respectively.

(d) What this model does not predict is runaway. With $r$ fixed, the deficit is bounded by $\Delta F/r$ however many cycles you run, so incomplete recovery alone produces a worse but stable joint. Runaway needs the loop of D10: the raised solid stress and friction must themselves degrade the matrix, lowering $r$ and raising $k$ on later cycles. That is the difference between a joint that is merely stiff and sore and one that is progressing, and it is why §8's threshold is a statement about a gain rather than about a number of steps.

import numpy as np

h, HA, mu_eq = 2e-3, 0.6e6, 0.15
lam = (2*np.arange(4000) + 1)*np.pi/2


def deficit(k, t=1.0):
    """1 - F(t): the fluid support lost in one loading."""
    return 1 - np.sum(2/lam**2 * np.exp(-lam**2 * HA*k*t/h**2))


def cycles(k, r, n=20):
    """Peak support at the end of each of n load/unload cycles."""
    dF, d, out = deficit(k), 0.0, []
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(1 - (d + dF))
        d = (1 - r)*(d + dF)
    return np.array(out)


for name, k, r in (("healthy ", 1e-15, 1.0), ("degraded", 1e-13, 0.8)):
    Fc = cycles(k, r)
    print(f"{name} dF={deficit(k):.4f}  F1={Fc[0]:.4f}  F5={Fc[4]:.4f}"
          f"  F20={Fc[19]:.4f}  F_inf={1 - deficit(k)/r:.4f}")

print("sweep r -> steady-state support and friction")
dFd = deficit(1e-13)
for r in (1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.5, 0.2):
    Finf = 1 - dFd/r
    print(f"  r={r:.1f}  F_inf={Finf:.4f}  mu_eff={mu_eq*(1 - Finf):.4f}"
          f"  ({1/r:.2f}x the single-step value)")
# healthy  dF=0.0138  F1=0.9862  F5=0.9862  F20=0.9862  F_inf=0.9862
# degraded dF=0.1382  F1=0.8618  F5=0.8273  F20=0.8273  F_inf=0.8273
# sweep r -> steady-state support and friction
#   r=1.0  F_inf=0.8618  mu_eff=0.0207  (1.00x the single-step value)
#   r=0.9  F_inf=0.8464  mu_eff=0.0230  (1.11x the single-step value)
#   r=0.8  F_inf=0.8273  mu_eff=0.0259  (1.25x the single-step value)
#   r=0.5  F_inf=0.7236  mu_eff=0.0415  (2.00x the single-step value)
#   r=0.2  F_inf=0.3090  mu_eff=0.1036  (5.00x the single-step value)
K10 — how much charge can cartilage afford to lose? Probes: inverting the Donnan formula for a mechanical criterion, and measuring the amplification K2 asserts (§2, §8).

The resting swelling pre-stress $\pi(c_F)=R_g\Theta\big(\sqrt{c_F^2+4c_0^2}-2c_0\big)$ keeps the matrix turgid; the extra effective stress needed to squeeze the drained matrix by a strain $\varepsilon$ is $H_A\varepsilon$. Call the tissue pre-stress-dominated while $\pi\gt H_A\varepsilon$. With $c_0=0.15\ \mathrm M$, $\Theta=310\ \mathrm K$, $H_A=0.6\ \mathrm{MPa}$: (a) verify that healthy cartilage ($c_F=0.2\ \mathrm M$) is pre-stress-dominated at $\varepsilon=0.10$, and by what factor. (b) Solve $\pi(c_F)=H_A\varepsilon$ numerically for the critical fixed-charge density $c_F^{\rm crit}$ at $\varepsilon=0.05,\,0.10,\,0.15$, and express each as a percentage of healthy. (c) Compute the logarithmic sensitivity $\partial\ln\pi/\partial\ln c_F$ at $c_F=0.2,\,0.1,\,0.05\ \mathrm M$ and reconcile it with D2's asymptotic limit and with K2's claim that the dependence is "steeper than linear". (d) Interpret: does losing charge degrade the tissue gracefully or abruptly?

solution

(a) $\pi(0.2\ \mathrm M)=0.1561\ \mathrm{MPa}$ against $H_A\varepsilon=0.6\times0.10=0.060\ \mathrm{MPa}$: the resting pre-stress is $2.60\times$ the stress a $10\%$ squeeze adds. Healthy cartilage is comfortably pre-stress-dominated — a pre-loaded structure, not a slack one.

(b) Root-finding $\pi(c_F)=H_A\varepsilon$ (the function is monotone in $c_F$, so bisection converges immediately): $c_F^{\rm crit}=0.0844\ \mathrm M$ at $\varepsilon=0.05$ ($42\%$ of healthy), $0.1205\ \mathrm M$ at $\varepsilon=0.10$ ($60\%$), $0.1489\ \mathrm M$ at $\varepsilon=0.15$ ($74\%$). Against a $10\%$ working strain the tissue crosses out of pre-stress dominance having lost only $40\%$ of its fixed charge — well inside the range K2's degeneration scenario covers.

(c) $\partial\ln\pi/\partial\ln c_F=1.832$ at $c_F=0.2\ \mathrm M$, $1.949$ at $0.1\ \mathrm M$, $1.986$ at $0.05\ \mathrm M$. The exponent climbs toward $2$ as $c_F$ falls, which is exactly D2's asymptotic limit $\pi\approx R_g\Theta c_F^2/(4c_0)$ reasserting itself once $c_F\ll c_0$. K2's "steeper than linear" is correct and now has a number: near the operating point the elasticity is $1.83$, so halving the charge costs a factor $2^{1.83}\approx3.6$ of swelling pressure — the $73\%$ loss K2 computes.

(d) Abruptly, and worse than abruptly: the sensitivity increases as the tissue degrades. The first $10\%$ of charge lost costs about $18\%$ of the pre-stress; by the time half is gone, each further increment costs nearly the square. A tissue losing charge slides down a curve that steepens under it. That is the osmotic half of §8's loop, and it is why the swelling pre-stress is the strut that fails first.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

RgTheta, c0, HA = 8.314*310, 0.15, 0.6e6      # J/mol, mol/L, Pa


def pi(cF):
    """Donnan swelling pressure [Pa]; cF, c0 in mol/L."""
    return RgTheta*(np.sqrt(cF**2 + 4*c0**2) - 2*c0)*1e3


print(f"(a) pi(0.2 M) = {pi(0.2)/1e6:.4f} MPa   HA*0.10 = "
      f"{HA*0.10/1e6:.3f} MPa   ratio {pi(0.2)/(HA*0.10):.2f}")

print("(b) critical fixed charge where pi = HA*eps")
for eps in (0.05, 0.10, 0.15):
    cc = brentq(lambda c: pi(c) - HA*eps, 1e-4, 1.0)
    print(f"    eps={eps:.2f}: cF_crit={cc:.4f} M  "
          f"({cc/0.2*100:.0f}% of healthy)")

print("(c) logarithmic sensitivity  d ln(pi) / d ln(cF)")
for cF in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05):
    dc = 1e-6
    num = np.log(pi(cF + dc)) - np.log(pi(cF - dc))
    den = np.log(cF + dc) - np.log(cF - dc)
    print(f"    cF={cF:.2f} M: {num/den:.3f}")
# (a) pi(0.2 M) = 0.1561 MPa   HA*0.10 = 0.060 MPa   ratio 2.60
# (b) critical fixed charge where pi = HA*eps
#     eps=0.05: cF_crit=0.0844 M  (42% of healthy)
#     eps=0.10: cF_crit=0.1205 M  (60% of healthy)
#     eps=0.15: cF_crit=0.1489 M  (74% of healthy)
# (c) logarithmic sensitivity  d ln(pi) / d ln(cF)
#     cF=0.20 M: 1.832
#     cF=0.10 M: 1.949
#     cF=0.05 M: 1.986

That closes the mechanics. The Appendix collects the notation and the parameter values used throughout; from here the course carries cartilage's stress, pressure, and flow fields forward into the full continuum treatment of Module 16 and the aging biology of Module 14.

Appendix — Notation and Parameters

This appendix collects, in one place, every symbol defined across §0–§9 and the healthy-adult-cartilage parameter values used throughout, with the section that introduces each. The mechanical foundations are Module 1 (force, stress, moment), the bone that backs the cartilage is Module 2, and the joint reaction that loads it comes from Module 3. The idealizations this module makes are cashed later by Module 16 (continuum / finite-element mechanics) and Module 14 (aging and osteoarthritis biology).

Notation

Symbols are grouped by role. Within the biphasic core, the one relation everything hangs from is the consolidation equation $\partial u/\partial t=H_Ak\,\partial^2u/\partial z^2$ of §3; the diffusivity $D=H_Ak$ and gel time $\tau=h^2/D$ derive from it.

SymbolMeaningIntroduced
Kinematics, stress, and fluid
$\varphi^s,\ \varphi^w$solid and fluid (water) volume fractions ($\varphi^s+\varphi^w=1$)§1
$h$cartilage layer thickness (the drainage path)§3
$u,\ \varepsilon$solid displacement and strain, $\varepsilon=\partial u/\partial z$§3
$v^s,\ v^w$solid- and fluid-phase velocities§3
$q$relative (Darcy) fluid flux, $q=-k\,\partial p/\partial z$§3
$p$interstitial (pore) fluid pressure§3, §4
$\sigma$total stress, $\sigma=\sigma_E-p$§3
$\sigma_E$solid effective (elastic) stress, $\sigma_E=H_A\varepsilon$§3
Transport and consolidation
$H_A$aggregate (confined-compression) modulus§3
$k$hydraulic permeability§3
$D$consolidation diffusivity, $D=H_Ak$§3
$\tau$gel (consolidation) time, $\tau=h^2/D$§3
$F$fluid load support fraction, $F(0)=1$§4
$T$dimensionless (diffusion) time, $T=Dt/h^2$; the absolute temperature is $\Theta$, below§4
$\lambda_n$drainage eigenvalues, $\lambda_n=(2n+1)\pi/2$ (one-sided)§4
Charge and osmotic (Donnan)
$c_F$fixed-charge density on the proteoglycans§2
$c_0$bath (external) salt concentration§2
$c_\pm$interstitial mobile cation / anion concentrations§2
$\pi$Donnan swelling (pre-stress) pressure§2
$R_g,\ \Theta$gas constant and absolute temperature ($R_g\Theta$ = thermal energy). Written $\Theta$, not $T$, because $T$ is the dimensionless time above§2
$\mathcal F$Faraday constant. Written $\mathcal F$, not $F$, because $F$ is the fluid load support fraction above§2
$W$body weight ($\approx686\ \mathrm N$ for the $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ reference human); joint loads are quoted as multiples of it§0
Contact and elasticity
$R$joint reaction force (from Module 3)§0
$R_{\rm eff}$effective (relative) radius of curvature of the contact§6
$E,\ \nu$instantaneous Young's modulus and Poisson ratio§6
$E^*$reduced (contact) modulus§6
$a,\ A_c$contact radius and contact area§6
$p_0,\ \bar p$peak (Hertz) and mean contact pressure§6
Lubrication and friction
$\mu$measured friction coefficient§7
$\mu_{\rm eq}$intrinsic (fully drained) friction coefficient§7
$\mu_{\rm eff}$effective friction, $\mu_{\rm eff}=\mu_{\rm eq}(1-F)$§7
$S$Stribeck number (bearing regime parameter)§7
$\eta$synovial fluid viscosity (shear-thinning)§7
$N$normal load across the contact (written $N$, not $W$, because $W$ is body weight)§7
$\mu_{\rm bl},\ S_0,\ \alpha$boundary plateau, transition and hydrodynamic slope of the classical Stribeck fit (all assumed)§7
$\kappa$intrinsic (geometric) permeability, $k=\kappa/\eta$; the pore-size factor $k$ carries alongside viscosity§1, §7
$E_a$Arrhenius activation energy (used here for water's viscosity, $16.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$)§7
$k_{\rm rate}$Module 0 §6's generic Arrhenius rate constant (kept apart from this module's permeability $k$)§7
Degeneration
$d$fluid-support deficit, $d=1-F$§8
$G$degeneration loop gain; the joint heals if $G\lt1$ and runs away if $G\gt1$§8
$[A]$mass concentration of intact, GAG-bearing aggrecan (same units as the GAG assay $m$ of §1)§8
$[\mathrm{Enz}]$active aggrecanase/MMP concentration (bracketed, not $E$, which is Young's modulus above)§8
$K_M,\ k_2$Michaelis constant and catalytic rate constant of Module 0 §6 Prop. 6.4 (kept apart from this module's permeability $k$)§8
$k_{\rm deg}$first-order aggrecan/charge decay rate, $k_{\rm deg}=k_2[\mathrm{Enz}]_{\rm tot}/K_M$§8
$\Lambda_\pi$local elasticity of swelling pressure w.r.t. fixed charge (written $\Lambda$, not $\varepsilon$, which is this module's strain)§8

These few numbers reproduce the whole module: $D=H_Ak$ gives the $\sim$hour gel time; $\tau\gg$ a footstep gives $F\approx1$ and near-frictionless contact; $\pi$ from $c_F$ gives the resting pre-stress and the overnight recovery; and their decay — rising $k$, falling $c_F$ — is the osteoarthritis cascade of §8, handed forward to Module 14 and Module 16.
